Seeing Differently: Modeling Interpretive Perspectives in Computational
Creativity using a Four-World Framework
Paper type: Study Paper
Prerna Luthra
Independent Researcher
prerna@samvedna.ai
Abstract
Creativity in computational systems is often evaluated
as an objective property of artifacts, with existing Com-
putational Creativity (CC) frameworks assessing cre-
ative merit at the level of outputs or systems rather than
interpretive context. However, artistic meaning is inher-
ently perspective-dependent and can vary across view-
ers and critical traditions. This paper proposes a com-
putational approach to modeling interpretive perspec-
tives rather than treating creativity as a single measur-
able construct. The study adopts a twelve-trait creativity
framework, organized across four conceptual domains,
and operationalizes it through three evaluative personas:
formalist, social-historical, and iconographic. Using
1,069 artworks from the SemArt dataset, the analysis
generates 38,484 persona-based evaluations to exam-
ine how perspectives shape creativity assessment. Re-
sults show systematic divergence across perspectives,
with traits such as Social Reflexivity exhibiting strong
viewpoint sensitivity. Linear probing of CLIP image
embeddings reveals that perspectives correspond to dis-
tinct orientation vectors in representation space, sug-
gesting that creativity evaluation depends on which vi-
sual features become salient under each persona condi-
tion. These findings support a relational view of cre-
ativity and indicate that incorporating multiple evalu-
ative perspectives could enable co-creative systems to
support interpretively diverse human collaborators.
Introduction
Computational approaches to creativity evaluation have
made substantial progress in operationalizing properties
such as novelty, value, and surprise as measurable attributes
of artifacts or systems (Boden 2004; Ritchie 2007). These

Child-centered and play-based education interventions, increasingly adopted worldwide, often aim to foster epistemic curiosity – the desire for new information – to enhance children’s learning. Dominant Western frameworks conceptualize curiosity as expressed through independent exploration and proactive questioning, treating these behaviors as prototypical indicators of curiosity. However, this characterization is largely derived from research in high-income Western contexts, raising concerns about its cross-cultural validity in non-Western low- and middle-income countries. This qualitative study examines how epistemic curiosity is expressed and interpreted in early childhood classrooms in Nepal. We analyzed data from focus groups with parents and child development experts, interviews with teachers, and classroom observations. Findings revealed expressions of curiosity that extend beyond Western prototypes, particularly attentive information-seeking, such as focused listening. These attentive behaviors were socially valued because they aligned with relational norms emphasizing respect and harmony. By conceptualizing curiosity as a universal construct with context-adaptive manifestations shaped by cultural and sociodemographic dynamics, this study advances a more inclusive …
